name: Taiping Rebellion
summary: In the 1840s Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka who had failed the imperial examinations and believed himself the younger brother of Jesus, gathered the God Worshipping Society in Guangxi. Famine, overtaxation and the Qing defeat in the First Opium War fed its growth, and in January 1851 Hong proclaimed the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom at Jintian. His armies marched north to the Yangtze, took Wuchang and in March 1853 captured Nanjing, which became their capital, Tianjing. An expedition against Beijing failed, and in 1856 a bloody power struggle killed several Taiping leaders. Provincial armies raised by gentry officials, above all Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army, slowly drove the Taiping back, while Western-officered forces helped defend Shanghai. In 1860 the Taiping broke out east into Jiangsu and Zhejiang, but the Qing took Anqing in 1861, besieged Nanjing from 1862 and stormed it in July 1864, shortly after Hong's death. It was the deadliest civil war in history and left the Qing dependent on regional armies.
casualties: An estimated 20–30 million people died, most of them from famine and disease; some estimates run far higher.

events.label: 11 Jan 1851
events.text: Hong Xiuquan proclaims the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom at Jintian
events.detail: In 1850 local officials in Guangxi moved against the God Worshipping Society, and its followers gathered at Jintian, near Guiping, organised into military units. After routing a Qing attack at the turn of the year, the God Worshippers formally rose on 11 January 1851, Hong Xiuquan's birthday, and declared the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. The rebels grew their hair long instead of wearing the Qing queue, a visible act of defiance that earned them the name 'Long-Hairs'.

events.label: 25 Sep 1851
events.text: Taiping break out of the Jintian area and take Yong'an
events.detail: Hemmed in by Green Standard troops that far outnumbered them, the rebels fought their way north and captured the walled town of Yong'an (modern Mengshan) on 25 September 1851. They held it for months while Qing forces regrouped and closed in, and in 1851 Hong gave his chief followers the title of king, under himself as Heavenly King. In 1852 the Taiping cut their way out and marched on Guilin, the provincial capital, but its walls proved too strong.

events.label: 10 Jun 1852
events.text: Ambush at Suoyi ford on the Xiang River halts the march into Hunan
events.detail: Leaving Guilin, the Taiping headed north towards Hunan along the Xiang River. On 10 June 1852 a gentry-led militia ambushed them at Suoyi ford, near Quanzhou on the Guangxi–Hunan border, and the rebels lost about a fifth of their force. The South King Feng Yunshan, one of the movement's founders, had been mortally wounded by a Qing gunner at nearby Quanzhou weeks earlier and died that June. The survivors pressed on into Hunan, recruiting as they went.

events.label: Sep 1852
events.text: Taiping besiege Changsha; the West King is killed
events.detail: The Taiping laid siege to Changsha, the capital of Hunan, which Qing reinforcements reached in time. Miners dug tunnels under the walls, but few reached them. In September the West King Xiao Chaogui, showing himself in royal robes to rally the troops, was killed by a Qing gunner. By November Hong called off the siege and the army moved north down the Xiang River towards Dongting Lake and the Yangtze, seizing thousands of boats at Yuezhou.

events.label: 12 Jan 1853
events.text: Taiping capture Wuchang on the Yangtze
events.detail: Reaching the Yangtze in December 1852, the Taiping first took the commercial towns of Hanyang and Hankou on the north bank, then bridged the river with boats to attack Wuchang, the capital of Hubei. After a siege of about twenty days the city fell on 12 January 1853. Warned of a large Qing army to the north, the leaders decided not to march on Beijing but to sail east down the Yangtze towards Nanjing, a choice later criticised as a strategic error.

events.label: 19 Mar 1853
events.text: Taiping take Nanjing and make it their Heavenly Capital
events.detail: Sailing down the Yangtze, the Taiping took Jiujiang and Anqing almost unopposed and reached Nanjing, the old southern capital, on 6 March 1853. Tunnels packed with explosives breached the walls and the city fell on 19 March. The Taiping killed tens of thousands of Manchu bannermen and their families in the garrison quarter. Hong renamed the city Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital, and ruled from there for eleven years, while Qing armies camped outside it.

events.label: 8 May 1853
events.text: Northern Expedition sets out to capture Beijing
events.detail: To strike at the Qing capital, the commander Yang Xiuqing sent an army under Lin Fengxiang and Li Kaifang north from Yangzhou on 8 May 1853. Moving fast through Anhui and Henan without leaving garrisons, it crossed the Yellow River in late June but then lost two months besieging Huaiqing. Turning through Shanxi into Zhili, it alarmed the court in Beijing, which called in Manchu and Mongol cavalry to defend the city.

events.label: 10 Jun 1853
events.text: Western Expedition retakes Anqing and pushes up the Yangtze
events.detail: A second army left Nanjing on 19 May 1853 to secure the Yangtze upstream. It recaptured Anqing on 10 June, then split: one force conquered much of Anhui and took Luzhou (Hefei) in January 1854, another went into Jiangxi, where it failed to take Nanchang, and a third moved on Hubei and Hunan. These campaigns gave the Taiping a belt of territory along the middle Yangtze that fed and recruited for the capital.

events.label: 30 Oct 1853
events.text: Northern Expedition turns towards Tianjin instead of Beijing
events.detail: Close to the capital by late October, the expedition did not attack Beijing but moved on Tianjin, where it waited for reinforcements through the north China winter. Its southern soldiers suffered badly from the cold and lack of supplies. On 5 February 1854 Li ordered a retreat south, and Qing generals broke dykes to flood the rebels. Historians often see the failure to strike at Beijing at once as one of the war's decisive mistakes.

events.label: 1 May 1854
events.text: Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army defeats the Taiping at Xiangtan
events.detail: Zeng Guofan, a senior official at home in Hunan, had turned local militia into a new provincial force, the Xiang (Hunan) Army, with its own river fleet and officers loyal to him personally. When Taiping forces of the Western Expedition took Xiangtan, upriver from Changsha, his troops beat them there on 1 May 1854. It was the first major victory of the new regional armies that would eventually win the war for the Qing.

events.label: 14 Oct 1854
events.text: Xiang Army retakes Wuchang and Hanyang
events.detail: Following up its victory at Xiangtan, the Xiang Army and its fleet pushed down the Xiang River and the Yangtze and recaptured Wuchang and Hanyang on 14 October 1854. The Taiping struck back: in 1855 Shi Dakai badly defeated Zeng's river fleet at Hukou, and Taiping forces took Wuchang again on 3 April 1855. The middle Yangtze changed hands repeatedly over the next two years.

events.label: May 1855
events.text: The last of the Northern Expedition is destroyed in Shandong
events.detail: After retreating from Tianjin, the expedition's two halves were trapped in fortified villages. Lin Fengxiang was captured in Zhili in March 1855, and Li Kaifang held out at Fengguantun in Shandong until Qing forces took him in spring 1855 (sources give 31 March or 31 May). Almost the whole army was lost. A relief force sent north from Anqing in 1854 had never reached it, and the Taiping did not threaten Beijing again.

events.label: 20 Jun 1856
events.text: Taiping break the Qing siege camp outside Nanjing
events.detail: Since 1853 a Qing army, the Jiangnan Battalion under Xiang Rong, had camped outside Nanjing. In June 1856 Taiping forces recalled from the west defeated it and lifted the three-year siege on 20 June; Xiang Rong died in August. The victory marked the height of Taiping power, holding the capital, much of Anhui and Jiangxi and the river between, but it also left the East King Yang Xiuqing feeling secure enough to claim equality with Hong.

events.label: 2 Sep 1856
events.text: Tianjing Incident: Taiping leaders kill each other in the capital
events.detail: When Yang Xiuqing demanded a title equal to Hong's, Hong summoned his generals. On 2 September 1856 Wei Changhui and Qin Rigang stormed Yang's palace and killed him, his family and thousands of his followers. Wei then turned on Shi Dakai, who escaped, and Hong had Wei and Qin killed in turn. More than 27,000 people died, and in 1857 Shi left Nanjing with a large army. The movement never recovered its unity or leadership.

events.label: 19 Dec 1856
events.text: Qing forces retake Wuchang for good
events.detail: While the Taiping leaders fought in Nanjing, Qing and Xiang Army forces besieging Wuchang took advantage. The city, which had changed hands several times since 1853, fell to the Qing on 19 December 1856 and stayed in their hands for the rest of the war. With Hubei secure, Zeng Guofan's armies could turn down the Yangtze towards Jiangxi and Anhui, the provinces that protected the Taiping capital.

events.label: May 1858
events.text: Xiang Army captures Jiujiang
events.detail: Jiujiang, at the mouth of Poyang Lake, had been a Taiping stronghold since 1853. In May 1858 the Xiang Army captured the city, and by September it had cleared the rest of Jiangxi. The fall of Jiujiang opened the Yangtze below Wuchang to Zeng's fleet and brought his armies to the borders of Anhui, the next province on the way to Nanjing.

events.label: 16 Nov 1858
events.text: Battle of Sanhe: Taiping destroy an elite Xiang Army force
events.detail: A Xiang Army column of about 6,000 under Li Xubin pushed into central Anhui in autumn 1858 and attacked the Taiping-held town of Sanhe, a supply hub west of Lake Chao. The Taiping generals Chen Yucheng and Li Xiucheng, two of the new commanders who rose after 1856, brought over 100,000 men and ambushed it on 16 November. Li Xubin and Zeng Guofan's brother were killed and the Qing siege of Anqing had to be abandoned.

events.label: May 1860
events.text: Taiping rout the Jiangnan Battalion and break out east
events.detail: A rebuilt Qing army again besieged Nanjing. To draw it off, Li Xiucheng raided Hangzhou in March 1860, then doubled back, and in May the Taiping routed the Jiangnan Battalion and lifted the siege. Hong Rengan, Hong's cousin and new chief minister, sent the armies east into southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang, the richest region of the empire. The Qing commanders Zhang Guoliang and He Chun died, and command passed to Zeng Guofan.

events.label: 2 Jun 1860
events.text: Taiping capture Suzhou
events.detail: Advancing down the Grand Canal, the Taiping took Changzhou on 26 May and Suzhou, one of China's wealthiest cities, on 2 June 1860. Li Xiucheng made Suzhou the seat of his own administration. In August a Taiping attack on Shanghai was repulsed by Chinese troops with European officers under the American Frederick Townsend Ward. The eastern campaign gave the Taiping a new heartland, but drew their best troops away from the middle Yangtze.

events.label: 5 Sep 1861
events.text: Xiang Army takes Anqing after a year-long siege
events.detail: Zeng Guofan saw Anqing, the Taiping base upstream of Nanjing, as the key to the river. His brother Zeng Guoquan besieged it from September 1860, while a British blockade stopped foreign merchants supplying the city. Chen Yucheng's attempts at relief failed, and on 5 September 1861 the besiegers breached the walls of the starving city. Zeng moved his headquarters to Anqing and prepared the advance on Nanjing.

events.label: 31 Dec 1861
events.text: Taiping capture Hangzhou and Ningbo in Zhejiang
events.detail: In late 1861 the Taiping launched a final eastern offensive. They took the treaty port of Ningbo on 9 December and, after a siege, Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang, on 31 December 1861. In January 1862 they surrounded Shanghai. The foreign powers, until then officially neutral, now joined the Qing in its defence, and Western naval forces and the Ever Victorious Army helped retake Ningbo on 10 May 1862.

events.label: May 1862
events.text: Xiang Army begins the siege of Nanjing
events.detail: Advancing down the Yangtze from Anqing, Zeng Guoquan's Xiang Army reached the walls of Nanjing in May 1862 and entrenched south of the city. Larger Taiping armies brought back from the east tried to break the siege but failed. Hong Xiuquan refused to leave, declaring that God would defend the Heavenly Capital, while Qing forces gradually took the river forts and the hills around the city.

events.label: 21 Sep 1862
events.text: Ward is mortally wounded at Cixi as Shanghai is held
events.detail: Around Shanghai, the Huai Army of Li Hongzhang, British and French troops and the Ever Victorious Army, a Western-officered Chinese force founded by the American Frederick Townsend Ward, drove Taiping forces back from the city in 1862. Ward was shot leading an attack on Cixi, near Ningbo, on 21 September 1862 and died the next day. In March 1863 command passed to the British officer Charles Gordon.

events.label: Dec 1863
events.text: Suzhou surrenders to Li Hongzhang and Gordon
events.detail: Through 1863 the Huai Army and Gordon's Ever Victorious Army took the towns between Shanghai and Suzhou, using armed steamers on the canals. In early December 1863 Taiping officers inside Suzhou killed their commander Tan Shaoguang and opened the gates. Li Hongzhang then had the surrendered Taiping leaders executed despite Gordon's guarantee of their safety, and Gordon briefly refused to fight on. The loss of Suzhou cost the Taiping their eastern capital.

events.label: 11 May 1864
events.text: Changzhou falls, completing the Qing reconquest of southern Jiangsu
events.detail: After Suzhou, the Huai Army and the Ever Victorious Army attacked Changzhou, the main Taiping base left on the Grand Canal. The decisive assault came between 25 April and 11 May 1864, when the city fell and its commander Chen Kunshu was captured and executed. In Zhejiang, Zuo Zongtang retook Hangzhou the same year. Gordon disbanded his army soon afterwards, and only Nanjing and scattered forces remained to the Taiping.

events.label: 1 Jun 1864
events.text: Hong Xiuquan dies in besieged Nanjing
events.detail: By March 1864 the Xiang Army had completed the encirclement of Nanjing, and food ran out inside. Hong Xiuquan fell ill after eating wild plants, possibly intending suicide, and died on 1 June 1864 after about twenty days. His fifteen-year-old son Hong Tianguifu succeeded him, and Li Xiucheng took charge of the defence, but during the siege more than 200,000 Taiping troops left the city to surrender.

events.label: 19 Jul 1864
events.text: Nanjing falls to the Xiang Army
events.detail: On 19 July 1864 the Xiang Army exploded a mine under the wall near the Taiping Gate and stormed into Nanjing; by evening every gate was taken. The unpaid troops looted, raped and killed, and the city burned for a week; Zeng Guofan's own reports put the dead at 100,000 or more. Li Xiucheng was captured and executed, and Hong's son was caught in October. Taiping remnants fought on in the south until 1866, but the Heavenly Kingdom was finished.

sources.title: Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864)

name: First Italo-Ethiopian War
summary: Italy had held the Red Sea port of Massawa since 1885 and built the colony of Eritrea on the plateau behind it. In 1889 Emperor Menelik II signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy, but its Italian text made Ethiopia an Italian protectorate while the Amharic text did not, and in 1893 Menelik repudiated it. In January 1895 Italian colonial troops under General Oreste Baratieri defeated Ras Mengesha of Tigray at Coatit and Senafe, then occupied Adigrat, Adwa and Mekelle and declared Tigray annexed. Menelik called up the nobility of the whole empire and marched north with an army of over 100,000, many armed with modern rifles. His forces overran an Italian outpost at Amba Alagi in December 1895 and forced the fort at Mekelle to surrender in January 1896. On 1 March 1896 Baratieri attacked near Adwa and his army was routed. In the Treaty of Addis Ababa of October 1896 Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence, a victory that became a symbol for anti-colonial and Pan-African movements.
casualties: At Adwa alone an estimated 6,000 Italian and colonial troops and 4,000–7,000 Ethiopians were killed; estimates for the whole war run to about 9,000 Italian and colonial dead and about 10,000 Ethiopian.

events.label: 13 Jan 1895
events.text: Italians repel Ras Mengesha's invasion of Eritrea at Coatit
events.detail: Menelik had repudiated the Treaty of Wuchale in 1893, and in December 1894 Bahta Hagos led a revolt against Italian rule in Eritrea, which was quickly crushed. Suspecting Ras Mengesha Yohannes, the ruler of Tigray, Governor Baratieri moved against him. Mengesha crossed into Eritrea with about 19,000 men, but on 13 January 1895 a colonial force of under 4,000, mostly Eritrean askaris, beat him at Coatit, opening the war.

events.label: 15 Jan 1895
events.text: Baratieri routs Mengesha's retreating army at Senafe
events.detail: Mengesha withdrew towards Tigray, but Baratieri caught up with his camp in the Senafe basin on the evening of 15 January 1895. Italian mountain guns shelled the camp from the heights over two days, and the Tigrayan army broke up with heavy losses. The defeat left Tigray open to invasion, and Baratieri gathered his troops at Senafe for an advance south across the border.

events.label: 25 Mar 1895
events.text: Italian troops occupy Adigrat in Tigray
events.detail: Crossing from Eritrea into the Ethiopian province of Tigray, Baratieri's army occupied the town of Adigrat on 25 March 1895. It became the main Italian base in Tigray, supporting further advances south. The Italians hoped that disaffected rulers such as Ras Mengesha, Negus Tekle Haymanot of Gojjam and the Sultan of Aussa would join them, but Ethiopia's nobility instead rallied to the emperor.

events.label: 2 Apr 1895
events.text: Italians occupy Adwa and declare Tigray annexed to Eritrea
events.detail: On 2 April 1895 Italian troops entered Adwa, the main town of western Tigray, and Baratieri issued a proclamation annexing Tigray to the colony of Eritrea. With the rainy season approaching, the Italians paused their advance. Menelik meanwhile sought help abroad, but France chose Italian goodwill over an alliance with him; Russia, which disliked a Catholic power ruling an Orthodox nation, sent arms.

events.label: 17 Sep 1895
events.text: Menelik II calls the Ethiopian nobility to war
events.detail: On 17 September 1895 Menelik issued a proclamation summoning the men of Ethiopia to join his army at Were Ilu. Regional rulers who had resented his rise, among them Ras Mengesha of Tigray, answered the call. Over the following months an army of more than 100,000 assembled and marched north, armed with tens of thousands of modern rifles bought from France, Russia and even Italy.

events.label: 9 Oct 1895
events.text: Italians push south past Debra Ailà and take Mekelle
events.detail: In October the Italians resumed their advance. On 9 October 1895 colonial battalions under General Giuseppe Arimondi drove Mengesha's rearguard from the pass of Debra Ailà, near Antalo. Mekelle, the Tigrayan capital, was occupied without a fight after Mengesha withdrew on Menelik's advice, and in October the Italians built a fort by the church of Enda Iyesus above the town. Advanced detachments went on south to the mountain stronghold of Amba Alagi.

events.label: 7 Dec 1895
events.text: Ethiopians overrun the Italian outpost at Amba Alagi
events.detail: Major Pietro Toselli held Amba Alagi with about 2,000 Eritrean askaris. On 7 December 1895 the vanguard of Menelik's army under Ras Makonnen, joined by Ras Mengesha and Ras Welle, attacked from several sides and overran the position. Toselli and most of his men were killed. Arimondi, coming up from Mekelle with reinforcements, could only collect a few hundred survivors and fall back north, leaving a garrison in the unfinished fort at Mekelle.

events.label: 18 Dec 1895
events.text: Ras Makonnen surrounds the Italian fort at Mekelle
events.detail: Major Giuseppe Galliano held the fort above Mekelle with about 1,150 askaris and 200 Italians and two mountain guns. Ras Makonnen's troops surrounded it on 18 December 1895 and a frontal assault a few days later was repulsed with heavy losses. Galliano was ordered to hold on while Baratieri concentrated the rest of the Italian army at Adigrat. In early January 1896 Menelik himself arrived with the main imperial army.

events.label: 21 Jan 1896
events.text: Mekelle garrison surrenders and is allowed to leave
events.detail: After two weeks of bombardment the Ethiopians cut the fort off from its water supply and beat back attempts to retake the well. With his men dying of thirst, Galliano agreed to surrender with his commanders' permission on 21 January 1896. Menelik let the garrison march out with its weapons and gave it mules to rejoin Baratieri. The escort also let the emperor move his army west, through passes the Italians did not guard, towards Adwa.

events.label: Feb 1896
events.text: Menelik moves on Adwa; Baratieri follows with his army
events.detail: Rather than attack the fortified Italian base at Adigrat, Menelik marched his army west by way of Hawzen to the plain around Adwa. Fearing an invasion of Eritrea, Baratieri left Adigrat and moved his army towards Adwa to face him. Both armies were short of food: the Ethiopian host had exhausted the countryside, while the Italians, at the end of a long supply line, had provisions for only a few more days.

events.label: 29 Feb 1896
events.text: Baratieri and his generals decide to attack
events.detail: On the evening of 29 February 1896 Baratieri, who knew he was about to be replaced by General Antonio Baldissera and was under pressure from Rome to win, met his four brigade commanders. With supplies running out, he suggested retreating towards Asmara, but the generals argued for an attack. Believing Menelik could field only about 30,000 men, Baratieri ordered an advance by night to positions overlooking the Ethiopian camp.

events.label: 1 Mar 1896
events.text: Battle of Adwa: Menelik's army routs the Italians
events.detail: About 17,700 Italian and Eritrean troops in four brigades marched overnight on separate mountain tracks and lost touch with each other. At dawn on 1 March 1896 Albertone's brigade ran into the Ethiopian army, perhaps 73,000 to 100,000 strong, and the others were attacked in turn and cut off. By noon the Italian army was in flight, abandoning its artillery. Over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and about 3,800 captured.

events.label: 10 Mar 1896
events.text: Crispi's government falls in Rome after the defeat
events.detail: News of Adwa reached Italy by telegraph almost at once and set off riots and demonstrations in several cities. Prime Minister Francesco Crispi, the main champion of colonial expansion in Ethiopia, was forced to resign, leaving office on 10 March 1896. Menelik offered peace if Italy publicly renounced its claim to a protectorate, but broke off talks when Italy asked for conditions. Talks went slowly while Italian prisoners remained in Ethiopian hands.

events.label: 18 May 1896
events.text: Italians evacuate Adigrat, their last foothold in Tigray
events.detail: General Baldissera reorganised the defeated army in Eritrea and relieved the Italian garrison left behind at Adigrat. Menelik insisted on its surrender as a condition of the peace talks, and on 18 May 1896 Baldissera evacuated the fort. The Italians withdrew behind the Mareb river, which became the border between Eritrea and Ethiopia, and Menelik returned to his capital, Addis Ababa.

events.label: 26 Oct 1896
events.text: Treaty of Addis Ababa: Italy recognises Ethiopian independence
events.detail: After months of negotiation, Italy agreed in August to abrogate the Treaty of Wuchale without conditions, and the Treaty of Addis Ababa was signed on 26 October 1896. Italy recognised Ethiopia's independence, paid for the upkeep of its prisoners and kept Eritrea up to the Mareb, Belesa and Muna rivers. Britain and France soon signed treaties treating Ethiopia as an equal, and it stayed independent until the Italian invasion of 1935.
